source_text: Libidinem ut pecorum, ita hominum fecit Deus; sed in pecoribus incoercitos dimisit affectus, in homine autem rationabili modum Deus instituit. Amictum ei prudentia et honestas comparat, quam dedit Deus. Igitur non modum, non genus; sed excessum eius culpat Deus, qui de insolentia liberae voluntatis exoriens, haud statum naturae, sed meritum agentis accusat.
pass_a_gloss: God made the lust of humans as of cattle; but in cattle he left the affections uncoerced, in the rational human however God instituted a measure. Prudence and honorableness, which God gave, furnish him a covering. Therefore God blames not the measure, not the genus; but its excess, which arising from the insolence of free will accuses not the status of nature but the desert of the agent.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS libido; Blaise pudenda libido vs nuptiae
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin
LS meritum; Blaise; glossary: desert not treasury-of-merit

pass_b_english: God made the lust of human beings just as he made that of animals. In animals he left the impulses unrestrained, but in rational human beings God established a limit. The prudence and decency God gave provide desire with a covering. Therefore God blames neither its proper measure nor its kind, but its excess. That excess arises from the unruliness of free will and accuses not nature’s condition but what the agent deserves.

choices.why: Julian's pudenda libido is the appetite accompanying union, not a created substance of sin.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
